subject: chemistry
title: Conservation of mass
key_idea: No atoms are made or lost in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. A mass change in an open container means a gas has entered or left.

sections.heading: The law of conservation of mass

blocks.text: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction. They are not created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same.

items.meaning: No atoms are made or lost in a reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
A container where nothing can enter or leave, such as a sealed flask.
A container that is open, so a gas can enter or leave.

items: In a closed system, the total mass before and after the reaction is the same.
A precipitation reaction in a closed flask shows no change in mass.
A balanced symbol equation also shows this. The total relative formula mass is the same on each side.

blocks.label: Mass is conserved
blocks.formula: mass of reactants = mass of products
where: Both masses are measured in grams (g).
Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The relative masses 48 + 32 = 80 are the same on each side of the arrow.

items: No atoms are made or lost, so total mass is unchanged.
In a closed system the mass before equals the mass after.

blocks.text: In an open container, a mass change usually means a gas has gone in or out. The gas still has mass, but it was not weighed.

items: A reaction in an open flask gives off a gas, such as carbon dioxide or hydrogen.
The gas **escapes** from the flask, so the mass shown on the balance falls.
Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate gives a metal oxide and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide escapes into the air.
A metal heated in air reacts with oxygen from the air.
The oxygen atoms add mass, so the metal oxide is heavier than the metal.
Example: copper + oxygen → copper oxide. The solid gains the mass of the oxygen it takes in.

blocks.label: Mass of a gas lost
blocks.formula: mass of gas lost = mass before − mass after
where: Both masses are the mass of the container and its contents, in grams (g).
Use this when the gas escapes from an open container.

diagram.alt: Calculate the mass of solid left after a gas escapes.
diagram.question: A student heats {start} g of copper carbonate in an open container. The reaction gives off {lost} g of carbon dioxide gas, which escapes. What is the mass of solid left?
working: Mass of solid left = mass before − mass of gas lost.

items: Mass falls in an open container when a gas escapes.
Mass rises when a solid reacts with a gas from the air, such as oxygen.
Always name the gas and say that it escapes or is taken in.

checks.q: State the law of conservation of mass.
checks.a: No atoms are made or lost in a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.

checks.q: Magnesium ribbon is heated in air. The mass of the solid increases. Explain why.
checks.a: Magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air. The oxygen atoms add mass to the solid magnesium oxide.

checks.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid in an open flask. Explain why the mass of the flask and contents falls.
checks.a: Hydrogen gas is produced and it escapes from the flask.

exam_phrases: (because) carbon dioxide is produced / carbon dioxide escapes (from the flask)
(oxygen is) a gas (which) escaped from the flask
the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants
no atoms were lost or made during the reaction
sum of relative formula masses on left hand side equals sum on right hand side

mistakes.wrong: The mass goes down because some of the reactants have disappeared.
mistakes.right: Name the gas and say it escapes. For example: carbon dioxide is produced and it escapes from the flask.

mistakes.wrong: The mass decreased because a gas was made.
mistakes.right: Making a gas is not enough. Add that the gas escapes from the flask (allowed: a gas is produced, for one mark).

mistakes.wrong: Show that the equation obeys the law by writing 'both sides have the same atoms'.
mistakes.right: Use the data. Add the relative formula masses on each side and show they are equal.

worked_example.question:
Tungsten oxide reacts with hydrogen to give tungsten (W) and water. The equation for the reaction is:

WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O

The law of conservation of mass states: 'The mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants during a chemical reaction.'

Relative atomic mass (Ar): W = 184
Relative formula masses (Mr): H₂ = 2, WO₃ = 232, H₂O = 18

Show that the equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.
answer_points: Both sides are equal, so the equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.
worked_example.tip: Multiply each Mr by its balancing number before adding. One mark is available for showing that both sides equal 238.

exam_phrases: escapes (from the flask) / released (from the flask)
oxygen atoms are added; oxygen atoms have mass
some copper oxide may be lost to air
mass of carbon dioxide = 5.000 − 2.800 = 2.20 (g) to 3 significant figures

mistakes.wrong: The mass falls because the magnesium reacts.
mistakes.right: References to magnesium reacting are ignored. Say that hydrogen (a gas) is formed and it escapes from the flask.
The mass of gas lost is a subtraction: 5.000 − 2.800 = 2.20 g. Dividing or adding the masses earns no final mark.
Where three significant figures are asked for, write 2.20 g. A value of 2.2 scores only the first mark.

worked_example.question:
The word equation for the reaction between magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid is

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

A strip of magnesium ribbon was placed in the conical flask. 100 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid was added to the conical flask.

The mass of the flask and contents was measured at regular intervals. The loss in mass was calculated.

Explain why there is a loss in mass of the flask and contents.
worked_example.tip: Both marks need linking: say what gas is formed, then say it escapes. References to magnesium reacting are ignored.

exam_phrases: No atoms are made or lost during a chemical reaction
the mass of the products is equal to the mass of the reactants
hydrogen is a gas / a gas is produced
the gas can escape (from the beaker)

mistakes.wrong: The mass of copper oxide is less because some gas escapes.
mistakes.right: Name the gas correctly. An incorrectly named gas is not allowed. In copper carbonate decomposition, carbon dioxide escapes.

mistakes.wrong: Mass is lost because the reaction uses up atoms.
mistakes.right: No atoms are made or lost in a reaction. Say that a gas is produced and escapes.

worked_example.question:
Two students heat some calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

Their results:

Mass of calcium carbonate (g) | Mass of calcium oxide (g) | Mass of carbon dioxide (g)
1.00 | 0.56 | 0.44
2.00 | 1.12 | 0.88
3.00 | 1.68 | 1.32
4.00 | 2.24 | ______

Student A states: 'If I heat 20 g of calcium carbonate, I will make 8.8 g of calcium oxide and 11.2 g of carbon dioxide.'

Is student A correct? Explain your answer.
answer_points: No. 20 g of calcium carbonate will make 11.2 g of calcium oxide (1).
And 8.8 g of carbon dioxide (1). The student has the numbers reversed.
worked_example.tip: Scale the table by 5. The calcium oxide mass is always larger than the carbon dioxide mass, and the two add up to the mass of calcium carbonate.
